set1.io: Differentiate obstructive and restrictive pulmonary patterns.
set1.q: A 60-year-old man's flow-volume loop (the smaller, inner loop) is shown against a normal loop. Which pattern does the inner loop show?
opts: Severe obstruction
Severe obstruction collapses the expiratory limb into a long flat tail; the inner loop is small but its limb is straight.
Restrictive
Correct. The inner loop keeps the normal shape, but everything is smaller: less volume is breathed in and out, the restrictive pattern.
Normal
The inner loop has the normal shape but covers far less volume than the normal loop around it.
Obstructive
Obstruction scoops the expiratory limb; the inner loop's limb runs straight, it is simply smaller.

set1.io: Differentiate obstructive and restrictive pulmonary patterns.
set1.q: A 63-year-old man's volume-time curve from a forced breath out is shown. Which pattern does it show?
opts: Obstructive
Correct. After a short first rise the curve flattens early into a slow climb that never reaches a plateau: the air leaves slowly, the obstructive pattern.
Restrictive
A restrictive curve keeps the normal shape, a steep rise and an early plateau, only at a lower volume; this one rises slowly and never levels off.
Gas transfer impairment
Gas transfer impairment has normal breathing mechanics, so its volume-time curve would look normal.
Normal
A normal curve rises steeply, with more than 80% of the forced vital capacity out in the first second, then plateaus.

set1.io: Describe pulmonary function testing parameters.
set1.q: A 24-year-old woman with asthma wants to check her expiratory airflow each morning at home. Which device fits?
opts: A calibration syringe
A calibration syringe keeps the testing equipment accurate; it measures nothing about the patient's own airflow.
A peak flow meter
Correct. A peak flow meter measures peak expiratory flow and is used at the bedside or at home, for example in asthma.
A blood gas analyzer
A blood gas analyzer measures gas exchange from a blood sample; it does not measure expiratory airflow.
A body plethysmograph
A body plethysmograph is a booth the patient sits in to measure lung volumes and airway resistance, not a device for daily home checks.

set1.io: Describe pulmonary function testing parameters.
set1.q: A 41-year-old woman's spirometry records how much air she forcefully blows out in the first second of a maximal breath out. Which value is this?
opts: Forced expiratory volume in 6 seconds
The forced expiratory volume in 6 seconds is the volume blown out by 6 seconds, not in the first second.
Peak expiratory flow rate
Peak expiratory flow rate is the maximum velocity of the forced breath out, a flow, not the volume of its first second.
Forced expiratory volume in one second
Correct. The forced expiratory volume in one second is the amount of air forcefully blown out in the first second of the breath out.
Forced vital capacity
The forced vital capacity is the TOTAL volume of the forced breath out, typically reached by about 6 seconds.

set1.io: Differentiate obstructive and restrictive pulmonary patterns.
set1.q: A 50-year-old woman with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis has spirometry. Which pattern of forced vital capacity and FEV1/FVC (forced expiratory volume in one second over forced vital capacity) ratio is expected?
opts: Decreased forced vital capacity, ratio below 70%
A low ratio with a low forced vital capacity is severe obstruction or a mixed defect; restriction keeps the ratio normal or high.
Normal forced vital capacity, ratio normal
A normal forced vital capacity with a normal ratio is normal lung mechanics; fibrosis decreases the forced vital capacity.
Normal forced vital capacity, ratio below 70%
A ratio below 70% is obstruction (here mild, with the forced vital capacity normal); fibrosis is restrictive.
Decreased forced vital capacity, ratio normal or high
Correct. In restrictive lung disease the forced vital capacity is decreased and the ratio is normal or increased (70% or more); the forced expiratory volume in one second is normal or decreased.

set1.io: Interpret basic pulmonary function study results.
set1.q: A 71-year-old man's FEV1/FVC (forced expiratory volume in one second over forced vital capacity) ratio is 50% (normal above 80%), and his forced vital capacity is 55% of predicted (normal 80% to 100%). What does the stepwise read of his spirometry give?
opts: Gas transfer impairment
Gas transfer impairment keeps normal breathing mechanics, but his ratio and forced vital capacity are both low.
Obstruction or a mixed defect
Correct. A low ratio with a low forced vital capacity reads as obstruction or mixed (severe obstruction can reduce the forced vital capacity too); the total lung capacity settles which.
Possible restriction
Restriction keeps the ratio normal or high; his ratio is low at 50%.
Normal lung mechanics
Normal mechanics needs a normal or high ratio and a normal forced vital capacity; both of his are low.

set1.io: Interpret basic pulmonary function study results.
set1.q: A 32-year-old woman who trains animals has had a progressive dry cough and dyspnea for a month, with fine crackles in both lungs. Her pulmonary function report is shown, with reference values. Which pattern does it show?
opts: Normal lung mechanics
Her forced vital capacity (39%) and total lung capacity (44% of reference) are far below normal.
Obstruction
Obstruction needs a ratio below 70%; hers is 94%, so her airflow out is not the problem.
Restriction

Correct. The FEV1/FVC (forced expiratory volume in one second over forced vital capacity) ratio is 94% against a reference of 84%, normal or high, and the forced vital capacity is low (39%): possible restriction, confirmed by a total lung capacity of 44%. The loop is narrow.
A mixed defect
A mixed defect needs a low ratio as well as a low total lung capacity; her ratio is high.

set1.io: Discuss indications for pulmonary function testing.
set1.q: A 38-year-old woman with an autoimmune disease feels well and breathes normally. Which reason for pulmonary function testing applies to her?
opts: Screening for an early, silent complication
Correct. Pulmonary function tests can screen for early, asymptomatic complications from non-pulmonary diseases such as autoimmune diseases.
Judging the prognosis of known lung disease
She has no known lung disease; the reason is screening for an early complication of her autoimmune disease.
Estimating risk before a lung resection
No resection is planned; the reason is screening for an asymptomatic complication of her autoimmune disease.
Diagnosing a symptomatic lung disease
She has no symptoms, so the diagnostic indication does not apply; screening for an early complication does.

set1.io: Describe pulmonary function testing parameters.
set1.q: A 48-year-old's report lists the average flow over the middle half of the forced vital capacity. Which value is this?
opts: Peak expiratory flow rate
Peak expiratory flow rate is the single maximum velocity of the forced breath out, not an average over its middle half.
Forced expiratory volume in 6 seconds
The forced expiratory volume in 6 seconds is the volume blown out by 6 seconds, not a flow.
Forced expiratory flow 25% to 75%
Correct. The forced expiratory flow 25% to 75% is the average flow from the point at which 25% of the forced vital capacity has been exhaled to the point at which 75% has.
Forced expiratory volume in one second
The forced expiratory volume in one second is a volume, blown out in the first second, not an average flow.

set1.io: Describe pulmonary function testing parameters.
set1.q: A 60-year-old woman's report lists the maximum volume of air her lungs can hold. Which volumes add up to it?
opts: Tidal and inspiratory reserve volumes
Those two make the inspiratory capacity, the breath that can be drawn in from the end of a quiet breath out.
Expiratory reserve and residual volumes
Those two make the functional residual capacity, the air left at the end of a quiet breath out.
All four volumes, residual volume included
Correct. Total lung capacity, the maximum volume the lungs can hold, is the sum of all four volumes: tidal, inspiratory reserve, expiratory reserve and residual.
Tidal volume and both reserve volumes
Those three make the vital capacity, which leaves out the residual volume that stays in the lungs.
set1.cite: Pulmonary Function Testing - Prof. Fowler.pptx, Slides 13 and 23

set1.io: Discuss indications for pulmonary function testing.
set1.q: A 66-year-old man has long-standing interstitial lung disease that is already diagnosed. Which use of pulmonary function testing applies to him?
opts: Judging the prognosis of his known disease
Correct. Pulmonary function tests can help determine the prognosis in a patient with known disease.
Screening for a silent complication
Screening is for early, asymptomatic complications of NON-pulmonary disease or medication; he has known lung disease.
Making his first diagnosis
His disease is already diagnosed, so the first-diagnosis indication no longer applies; prognosis does.
Naming the specific cause of his disease
Pulmonary function tests do not provide a specific diagnosis; they show the derangement the disease causes.

set1.io: Describe pulmonary function testing parameters.
set1.q: A 50-year-old woman completes three acceptable spirometry efforts. Which values go in her report?
opts: The values from the final effort
The last effort is not the one kept; of the three, the highest volumes and flows are recorded.
The highest volumes and flows of the three
Correct. Spirometry is repeated three times, and the highest air volumes and flows are the ones recorded.
The lowest values, as the safest estimate
The lowest effort underestimates the lungs; the highest volumes and flows of the three are recorded.
The average of the three efforts
The efforts are not averaged: the highest volumes and flows of the three are recorded.
set1.cite: Pulmonary Function Testing - Prof. Fowler.pptx, Slide 24

set1.io: Explain the role of pulmonary function testing in diagnosis and monitoring of pulmonary disease.
set1.q: A 68-year-old woman with interstitial lung disease has started treatment. Which specialized test is used to monitor her response to treatment and her prognosis?
opts: Maximal inspiratory and expiratory pressures
Those measure diaphragmatic strength and the neurologic side of breathing, not response to treatment.
An arterial blood gas
An arterial blood gas is another specialized test, but the one used to monitor treatment response and prognosis is the six-minute walk test.
Peak flow measurement
Peak flow measures maximum expiratory airflow in a single breath, as in asthma; treatment response and prognosis are monitored by the six-minute walk test.
Six-minute walk test
Correct. The six-minute walk test (walking as far as possible in 6 minutes) is used to monitor response to treatment as well as prognosis.

set1.io: Interpret basic pulmonary function study results.
set1.q: A 63-year-old man's forced vital capacity is 35% of predicted and his FEV1 (forced expiratory volume in one second) is 49% of predicted (both normal 80% to 100%); his FEV1/FVC (forced expiratory volume in one second over forced vital capacity) ratio is 98%, with a predicted value of 69%. Which pattern does this spirometry suggest?
opts: Possible restriction
Correct. The ratio is normal or high (98%) and the forced vital capacity is low (35% of predicted): the stepwise read gives possible restriction, to be confirmed by the total lung capacity.
Normal lung mechanics
A forced vital capacity of 35% of predicted is far below normal.
A mixed defect
A mixed defect needs a LOW ratio as well as a low total lung capacity; his ratio is high.
Obstruction
Obstruction is a ratio below 70%; his ratio is 98%, the opposite end of the scale.

set1.io: Differentiate obstructive and restrictive pulmonary patterns.
set1.q: A 69-year-old woman's flow-volume loop is shown. Which pattern does it show?
opts: Normal
A normal expiratory limb falls in a straight line from the peak; this one is scooped inward.
Restrictive
A restrictive loop is narrow and tall with a sharp point, everything smaller; this loop is wide with a scooped expiratory limb.
Gas transfer impairment
Gas transfer impairment keeps normal breathing mechanics, so its loop would look normal.
Obstructive
Correct. After its peak the expiratory limb is scooped inward (coving) and trails out slowly: a scoop in the loop is the shape of obstruction.
set1.cite: Pulmonary Function Testing - Prof. Fowler.pptx, Slides 44 and 9

set1.io: Describe pulmonary function testing parameters.
set1.q: A 58-year-old man with dyspnea needs his total lung capacity and his residual volume measured. Which test measures both?
opts: Exercise oximetry
Exercise oximetry follows oxygenation at rest and with modest activity; it measures no lung volume at all.
Whole-body plethysmography
Correct. Whole-body plethysmography measures the total lung capacity, the functional residual capacity, the residual volume and airway resistance.
Maximal inspiratory pressure testing
Maximal inspiratory and expiratory pressures measure diaphragmatic strength and the neurologic side of breathing, not lung volumes.
A peak flow meter
A peak flow meter measures peak expiratory flow at the bedside or at home; it gives no lung volume such as the total lung capacity.

set1.io: Discuss pulse oximetry and oxygenation assessment.
set1.q: A 72-year-old man with COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) is short of breath when he walks. Which quick, inexpensive test checks his oxygenation at rest and with modest activity?
opts: Whole-body plethysmography
Plethysmography measures lung volumes and airway resistance, not oxygenation with activity.
Exercise oximetry
Correct. Exercise oximetry checks oxygenation at rest and with modest activity, and it is quick and cheap.
Diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide
The diffusing capacity tests the alveolar-capillary membrane; it does not follow oxygenation during activity.
An arterial blood gas
An arterial blood gas is a specialized test from a blood sample; the quick, cheap check at rest and with activity is exercise oximetry.
set1.cite: Pulmonary Function Testing - Prof. Fowler.pptx, Slides 19 and 13

set1.io: Differentiate obstructive and restrictive pulmonary patterns.
set1.q: A 62-year-old former smoker has dyspnea on exertion, wheezing and this chest film, hyperinflated with flat diaphragms. Which pulmonary function pattern is expected?
opts: Obstructive
Correct. A former smoker with wheezing fits chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or asthma, both obstructive (increased airway resistance), and the film is hyperinflated with flattened diaphragms.
Gas transfer impairment
Gas transfer impairment keeps normal mechanics; wheezing in a former smoker points to increased airway resistance.
Restrictive
Restriction gives small-volume lungs, as with reticular opacities and Velcro crackles; this film is hyperinflated.
Normal lung mechanics
Wheezing, dyspnea and a hyperinflated film in a former smoker are not normal mechanics; they fit obstruction.

set1.io: Differentiate obstructive and restrictive pulmonary patterns.
set1.q: A 54-year-old woman's volume-time curve (the lower curve) is shown against a normal one. Which pattern does the lower curve show?
opts: Normal
The shape is normal, but the curve plateaus at a clearly lower volume than the normal one above it.
Severe obstruction
Severe obstruction rises slowly and never reaches a plateau; this curve plateaus early.
Restrictive
Correct. The lower curve has the normal shape, a steep rise and an early plateau, but reaches less volume: the air comes out easily, there is simply less of it, the restrictive pattern.
Obstructive
An obstructive curve rises slowly and takes longer to plateau; this one rises steeply and plateaus early, only lower.

set1.io: Differentiate obstructive and restrictive pulmonary patterns.
set1.q: A 57-year-old's volume-time curve and flow-volume loop are shown, each against a dashed normal outline. Which pattern do they show?
opts: Restriction
Restriction plateaus at the normal time but at a lower volume; this curve reaches the normal volume, only late.
Normal
A normal curve plateaus early and the loop has no coving; here the plateau is late and the limb is scooped.
Severe obstruction
Severe obstruction never reaches a plateau, the forced vital capacity is reduced and the peak severely reduced; this curve does reach the normal volume.
Mild obstruction

Correct. The volume-time curve reaches its plateau late but still reaches the normal volume (the forced vital capacity is preserved), and the loop shows coving with a mildly reduced peak: mild obstruction.

set1.io: Describe pulmonary function testing parameters.
set1.q: A 30-year-old man breathes quietly at rest while his breathing is recorded. What is the volume of air he moves in and out with each restful breath called?
opts: Functional residual capacity
Functional residual capacity is the air left in the lungs at the end of a quiet breath out, not the air moved.
Tidal volume
Correct. Tidal volume is the air moved in and out with each normal restful breath, about 500 mL depending on age, sex and size.
Inspiratory reserve volume
The inspiratory reserve volume is the extra air breathed in on top of the tidal volume, not the restful breath itself.
Vital capacity
Vital capacity is the tidal volume plus both reserve volumes: the fullest breath in and out, not a quiet breath.
set1.cite: Pulmonary Function Testing - Prof. Fowler.pptx, Slides 21 and 23

set1.io: Describe pulmonary function testing parameters.
set1.q: A 40-year-old has this tracing of quiet breaths, one deepest breath in and one fullest breath out. Which volume is shaded?
opts: Tidal volume
Tidal volume is the small rise and fall of each quiet breath, which sits above the shaded band.
Expiratory reserve volume
Correct. The shaded band runs from the end of a quiet breath out down to the lowest point of the fullest breath out: the additional volume that can be breathed out, the expiratory reserve volume.
Residual volume
Residual volume lies below the lowest point of the tracing: the air still in the lung after maximal expiration.
Functional residual capacity
Functional residual capacity is the shaded band plus the residual volume beneath it: all the air left at the end of a quiet breath out.

set1.io: Interpret basic pulmonary function study results.
set1.q: A 59-year-old man's spirometry report lists his FEV1 (forced expiratory volume in one second), his FVC (forced vital capacity), their ratio and his total lung capacity. Which should be assessed first in a stepwise read?
opts: The total lung capacity
The total lung capacity confirms restriction or a mixed defect after the spirometry read; it is not the first step.
The forced vital capacity
The forced vital capacity is the second step, read in the light of the ratio (low or normal-to-high).
The forced expiratory volume in one second
The forced expiratory volume in one second alone can be normal or decreased in both patterns; the read starts with the ratio.
Their ratio
Correct. The stepwise read assesses the ratio of the forced expiratory volume in one second to the forced vital capacity first; the forced vital capacity comes next.

set1.io: Differentiate obstructive and restrictive pulmonary patterns.
set1.q: A 35-year-old man's flow-volume loop is shown. How is the shape read?
opts: Severe obstruction
Severe obstruction has a low peak and a deeply scooped expiratory limb; this peak is high and the limb straight.
Restrictive
A restrictive loop is narrow and small, like a witch's hat; this one has normal width.
Normal
Correct. A quick rise to a sharp peak, then an expiratory limb that falls in a straight line to the volume axis, and a rounded inspiratory limb below: the normal loop.
Obstructive
Obstruction scoops the expiratory limb inward (coving); this limb falls in a straight line.

set1.io: Describe pulmonary function testing parameters.
set1.q: A 38-year-old's flow-volume loop from spirometry is shown. What does the arrowhead at the top of the loop mark?
opts: Tidal volume
Tidal volume is a quiet breath; this loop records a maximal forced breath, and its top is the peak expiratory flow.
Forced expiratory volume in one second
The forced expiratory volume in one second is marked further along the expiratory limb (the vertical line), not at the loop's peak.
Forced vital capacity
The forced vital capacity is the total volume of the forced breath out, read along the volume axis, not the flow at the loop's top.
Peak expiratory flow
Correct. The top of the expiratory limb is the peak expiratory flow: the maximum velocity reached during the forced breath out.

set1.io: Explain the role of pulmonary function testing in diagnosis and monitoring of pulmonary disease.
set1.q: A 54-year-old smoker with wheezing may have obstructive lung disease. Which standard test is responsible for diagnosing it?
opts: Diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide
The diffusing capacity diagnoses pulmonary vascular disease by testing the alveolar-capillary membrane.
Lung volume measurement
Lung volumes are responsible for diagnosing restrictive disease, not obstruction.
An arterial blood gas
An arterial blood gas is a specialized test, not the standard test for obstruction, which is spirometry.
Spirometry with a flow-volume loop
Correct. Spirometry, including the flow-volume loop, is the standard test responsible for diagnosing obstructive lung disease.

set1.io: Describe pulmonary function testing parameters.
set1.q: A 45-year-old's report lists his inspiratory capacity. Which volumes does this capacity combine?
opts: Tidal volume and inspiratory reserve volume
Correct. Inspiratory capacity is the sum of the tidal volume and the inspiratory reserve volume.
All four lung volumes
All four volumes together, the residual volume included, make the total lung capacity.
Tidal volume and both reserve volumes
Tidal volume plus both reserve volumes is the vital capacity, which also includes the air breathed out.
Expiratory reserve volume and residual volume
Those two make the functional residual capacity, the air left in the lungs at the end of a quiet breath out.

set1.io: Discuss pulse oximetry and oxygenation assessment.
set1.q: A 58-year-old man's clinician needs his pH and his oxygen and carbon dioxide partial pressures. Which piece of pulmonary function equipment reports these values?
opts: A peak flow meter
A peak flow meter measures peak expiratory flow, at the bedside or at home, not gas exchange.
A pulse oximeter
A pulse oximeter clips on the fingertip and reads the oxygen saturation and the pulse rate, not the pH or the partial pressures.
A blood gas analyzer

Correct. The blood gas analyzer is the pulmonary function equipment whose readout gives the pH and the partial pressures of carbon dioxide and oxygen, with bicarbonate: it measures gas exchange and oxygenation.
A body plethysmograph
A body plethysmograph is the booth that measures lung volumes and airway resistance, not blood gases.

set1.io: Interpret basic pulmonary function study results.
set1.q: A 69-year-old man's FEV1/FVC (forced expiratory volume in one second over forced vital capacity) ratio is 52% (normal above 80%), and his total lung capacity is 65% of predicted (normal 80% to 120%). What is the basic interpretation?
opts: Restriction alone
A low total lung capacity alone is restriction, but his low ratio adds obstruction.
Normal lung mechanics
Both his ratio and his total lung capacity are below their normal ranges.
A mixed defect
Correct. A low ratio (obstruction) together with a low total lung capacity (restriction) is obstruction and restriction: a mixed defect.
Obstruction alone
A low ratio alone is obstruction, but his total lung capacity is low as well, which adds restriction.

set1.io: Differentiate obstructive and restrictive pulmonary patterns.
set1.q: A 38-year-old woman with severe scoliosis has dyspnea on exertion. Which pulmonary function pattern is expected?
opts: Restrictive
Correct. Chest wall pathology (obesity, kyphosis, scoliosis) gives restrictive physiology: the lungs need more effort to expand than normal, and the breaths are shallow.
Obstructive
Obstruction is increased airway resistance, as in asthma or cystic fibrosis; scoliosis restricts expansion of the chest instead.
Gas transfer impairment
Gas transfer impairment has normal breathing mechanics; a deformed chest wall disturbs the mechanics themselves.
Normal lung mechanics
A chest wall that limits expansion is not normal mechanics; scoliosis is listed with the restrictive chest wall diseases.

set2.io: Describe pulmonary function testing parameters.
set2.q: A 44-year-old's volume-time curve from spirometry is shown. What does the marked point represent?
opts: Forced vital capacity
The forced vital capacity is the plateau the curve reaches, the maximum volume, typically by about 6 seconds, not the point at 1 second.
Forced expiratory volume in 6 seconds
The forced expiratory volume in 6 seconds would be read at 6 seconds on the time axis; the marked point sits at 1 second.
Peak expiratory flow rate
Peak expiratory flow rate is the maximum slope of the curve, its steep first rise, not a point on it.
Forced expiratory volume in one second
Correct. The point sits at 1 second on the time axis: the volume exhaled in the first second of the forced breath, the forced expiratory volume in one second.

set2.io: Describe pulmonary function testing parameters.
set2.q: A 26-year-old woman breathing quietly is told to take the deepest breath she can. Which volume is the extra air she draws in above a normal breath?
opts: Inspiratory capacity
Inspiratory capacity is the tidal volume plus the inspiratory reserve volume; the extra air alone is the reserve volume.
Inspiratory reserve volume
Correct. The inspiratory reserve volume is the additional volume breathed in on top of the tidal volume.
Total lung capacity
Total lung capacity is all four volumes together, the residual volume included, not just the extra breath in.
Expiratory reserve volume
The expiratory reserve volume is the extra air breathed OUT after a normal breath, the opposite direction.

set2.io: Discuss indications for pulmonary function testing.
set2.q: A 67-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is being considered for a lung resection. Why would pulmonary function tests be ordered before surgery?
opts: To give a specific diagnosis
Pulmonary function tests do not provide a specific diagnosis; here they estimate how much surgical risk she carries.
To measure her oxygen saturation
Oxygen saturation is measured by pulse oximetry; pulmonary function tests before resection estimate surgical risk.
To estimate her surgical risk
Correct. Pulmonary function tests can be used to estimate surgical risk in patients facing lung resection or with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
To screen for amiodarone toxicity
Screening for drug toxicity applies to a patient on a drug such as long-term amiodarone; her question is surgical risk.

set2.io: Differentiate obstructive and restrictive pulmonary patterns.
set2.q: A 74-year-old woman's flow-volume loop is shown. Which pattern does it show?
opts: Mild obstruction
Mild obstruction keeps a nearly normal peak (only mildly reduced) with slight coving; here the peak is low and the limb collapses.
Restriction
A restrictive loop is narrow with a sharp, high point and a straight limb; this one is wide with a collapsed limb.
Normal
A normal loop reaches a high peak and falls in a straight line; this limb is deeply scooped.
Severe obstruction
Correct. The peak is low and the expiratory limb collapses almost at once into a long, flat tail: deep coving with a severely reduced peak expiratory flow, the loop of severe obstruction.

set2.io: Interpret basic pulmonary function study results.
set2.q: A 35-year-old man's FEV1/FVC (forced expiratory volume in one second over forced vital capacity) ratio is 85% (normal above 80%), and his forced vital capacity is 96% of predicted (normal 80% to 100%). How is this read?
opts: Obstruction
Obstruction needs a low ratio, below 70%; his is 85%, so the read stays on the normal branch.
Normal lung mechanics
Correct. A normal or high ratio with a normal or high forced vital capacity reads as normal lung mechanics.
Possible restriction
Possible restriction needs a LOW forced vital capacity with the normal or high ratio; his is 96%.
A mixed defect
A mixed defect needs a low ratio and a low total lung capacity; his ratio is normal.

set2.io: Describe pulmonary function testing parameters.
set2.q: A 34-year-old man takes a maximal breath and then blows out forcefully and rapidly until he can blow out no more. What is the total volume he exhales called?
opts: Total lung capacity
Total lung capacity also includes the residual volume, which stays in the lungs after the hardest breath out.
Forced expiratory volume in one second
That is only the part blown out in the first second, not the total volume of the forced breath.
Forced vital capacity
Correct. The forced vital capacity is the total volume a person can forcefully and rapidly exhale after a maximal deep breath, typically reached by about 6 seconds.
Peak expiratory flow rate
Peak expiratory flow rate is the maximum speed of the forced breath out, a flow rather than a volume.

set2.io: Interpret basic pulmonary function study results.
set2.q: A 48-year-old woman's FEV1/FVC (forced expiratory volume in one second over forced vital capacity) ratio is 58% (normal above 80%), and her forced vital capacity is 92% of predicted (normal 80% to 100%). How is this read?
opts: Possible restriction
Possible restriction is a normal or high ratio with a low forced vital capacity; her ratio is low.
A mixed defect
A mixed defect needs a low total lung capacity as well; a low ratio with a normal forced vital capacity reads as obstruction.
Obstruction
Correct. A low ratio sends the read to the forced vital capacity; a normal forced vital capacity with a low ratio reads as obstruction.
Normal lung mechanics
Normal lung mechanics needs a normal or high ratio; hers is 58%.

mis.A mixed defect: needs a low forced vital capacity and total lung capacity

set2.io: Describe pulmonary function testing parameters.
set2.q: A 47-year-old woman sits inside a glass booth for whole-body plethysmography. Besides her lung volumes, which measure does this test report?
opts: Airway resistance
Correct. Whole-body plethysmography also reports airway resistance: how hard it is for air to flow through the bronchial tubes.
Peak expiratory flow
Peak expiratory flow comes from a peak flow meter or spirometry; plethysmography adds airway resistance to the lung volumes.
Oxygen saturation
Oxygen saturation comes from a pulse oximeter; plethysmography reports the lung volumes and airway resistance.
Diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide
The diffusing capacity is its own standard test, of the alveolar-capillary membrane; plethysmography reports lung volumes and airway resistance.

set2.io: Discuss indications for pulmonary function testing.
set2.q: A 64-year-old man has taken amiodarone for years and has no breathing symptoms. Why might pulmonary function tests be ordered?
opts: To screen for early pulmonary toxicity

Correct. Pulmonary function tests can screen for early, asymptomatic complications of non-pulmonary disease or medication, such as long-term amiodarone, which can cause significant pulmonary toxicity.
To diagnose the cause of his symptoms
He has no breathing symptoms; the indication is screening for an early, asymptomatic complication of his medication.
To judge the prognosis of a lung disease
He has no known lung disease whose prognosis is in question; the reason is screening for drug toxicity.
To estimate his risk before lung surgery
No lung surgery is planned; the reason here is screening for amiodarone pulmonary toxicity.
set2.cite: Pulmonary Function Testing - Prof. Fowler.pptx, Slide 5

set2.io: Differentiate obstructive and restrictive pulmonary patterns.
set2.q: A 49-year-old's volume-time curve and flow-volume loop are shown, each against a dashed normal outline. Which pattern do they show?
opts: Mild obstruction
Mild obstruction plateaus late with the forced vital capacity preserved, and its loop shows coving; this one plateaus normally, lower.
Restriction
Correct. The volume-time curve plateaus normally but at a lower volume (the forced vital capacity is reduced), and the loop is smaller with a normal or mildly reduced peak and no coving: restriction.
Severe obstruction
Severe obstruction never reaches a plateau and has a deeply coved loop; this curve plateaus normally.
Normal
The shape is normal, but the plateau and the loop stop short of the dashed normal outline.

set2.io: Describe pulmonary function testing parameters.
set2.q: A 57-year-old man's spirometry report includes a graph plotting airflow against lung volume during a forced breath in and out. What is this graph called?
opts: A tracing of quiet breaths
A tracing of quiet and deep breaths shows the lung volumes and capacities over time; it does not plot flow against volume.
A flow-volume loop
Correct. The flow-volume loop plots airflow speed against lung volume during a forced inhalation and expiration in spirometry.
A volume-time curve
A volume-time curve plots exhaled volume against time; flow appears only as its slope, not on an axis.
A peak flow meter reading
A peak flow meter gives one peak expiratory flow number, not a graph of flow across the whole breath.
set2.cite: Pulmonary Function Testing - Prof. Fowler.pptx, Slides 26, 30, 20 and 15

set2.io: Interpret basic pulmonary function study results.
set2.q: A 56-year-old smoker has had a productive cough and dyspnea for 3 months, with diminished breath sounds. His pulmonary function report is shown, with reference values. How is the report read?
opts: Obstruction

Correct. The FEV1/FVC (forced expiratory volume in one second over forced vital capacity) ratio is low (52% against a reference of 82%); the forced vital capacity is low too (61%), so obstruction or mixed; the total lung capacity of 120% is not low, so this is obstruction. The loop is scooped.
A mixed defect
A mixed defect needs a low total lung capacity as well as a low ratio; his total lung capacity is 120% of reference.
Restriction
Restriction needs a normal or high ratio and a low total lung capacity; his ratio is 52% and his total lung capacity 120%.
Normal lung mechanics
A ratio of 52% against a reference of 82% is not normal mechanics.

set2.alt: Pulmonary function report with spirometry, lung volumes, diffusing capacity and a small flow-volume loop

mis.A mixed defect: needs a low total lung capacity

set2.io: Interpret basic pulmonary function study results.
set2.q: A 57-year-old woman's total lung capacity is 62% of predicted (normal 80% to 120%), with an FEV1/FVC (forced expiratory volume in one second over forced vital capacity) ratio of 88% (normal above 80%). What is the basic interpretation?
opts: Normal lung mechanics
A total lung capacity of 62% is well below the normal 80% to 120%, so this is not normal.
A mixed defect
A mixed defect is a low ratio AND a low total lung capacity; her ratio is normal.
Restriction
Correct. A low total lung capacity is restriction, and her ratio is normal, so there is no obstruction alongside it.
Obstruction
Obstruction is a low ratio, below 70%; hers is 88%, so obstruction is not part of this picture.
set2.cite: Pulmonary Function Testing - Prof. Fowler.pptx, Slides 43 and 32

set2.io: Discuss pulse oximetry and oxygenation assessment.
set2.q: A 79-year-old woman with lung disease is sent home with a small clip-on fingertip device to check her oxygenation. Which device is it?
opts: A pulse oximeter
Correct. A pulse oximeter is the pulmonary function equipment that measures oxygenation, small enough for home use.
A handheld spirometer
A handheld spirometer measures airflow and some lung volumes, not oxygenation.
A peak flow meter
A peak flow meter measures peak expiratory flow, not oxygenation, though it too is used at home.
A blood gas analyzer
A blood gas analyzer measures gas exchange from a blood sample on a benchtop machine, not from a fingertip clip.

set2.io: Differentiate obstructive and restrictive pulmonary patterns.
set2.q: A 66-year-old man with emphysema has a decreased FEV1/FVC (forced expiratory volume in one second over forced vital capacity) ratio. Why does the ratio fall in obstruction?
opts: The first-second volume drops more than the total volume

Correct. The ratio is the percentage of the forced vital capacity exhaled in the first second; in obstruction it falls below 70% because the forced expiratory volume in one second drops proportionally more than the forced vital capacity.
The total lung capacity falls below normal
A low total lung capacity marks restriction; it is not part of this ratio, which is built from the two forced values.
The total volume drops more than the first-second volume
That would keep the ratio normal or raise it, as in restriction, where the forced vital capacity is the value that is decreased.
Both fall by exactly the same proportion
An equal fall would leave the ratio unchanged; in obstruction the ratio drops below 70%.
set2.cite: Pulmonary Function Testing - Prof. Fowler.pptx, Slides 26, 41 and 43

set2.io: Describe pulmonary function testing parameters.
set2.q: A 45-year-old man is coached through spirometry. After he breathes in as deeply as he can, what is he asked to do?
opts: Blow out as hard and fast as he can for 6 seconds or more
Correct. After a maximal breath in, the patient exhales forcefully, as fast as possible, and keeps going for at least 6 seconds.
Breathe quietly through the mouthpiece for a minute
Quiet breathing shows only the tidal volume; spirometry needs the maximal breath in and then the forceful breath out.
Breathe out slowly and gently until the breath is empty
A slow, gentle breath out cannot show how fast air leaves the lungs; spirometry needs a forceful, fast exhalation for at least 6 seconds.
Blow out hard for one second, then stop
Stopping after one second captures only the first-second volume; the effort continues for at least 6 seconds so the forced vital capacity is reached.
set2.cite: Pulmonary Function Testing - Prof. Fowler.pptx, Slides 24, 29 and 21

set2.io: Explain the role of pulmonary function testing in diagnosis and monitoring of pulmonary disease.
set2.q: A 61-year-old man has diffuse lung disease of uncertain type. Into which three categories do pulmonary function tests help classify it?
opts: Infectious, neoplastic and inflammatory
Pulmonary function tests show physiology, not cause, and do not provide a specific diagnosis; the three categories are obstructive, restrictive and pulmonary vascular.
Large airway, small airway and alveolar
Those are parts of the system the tests examine; the disease categories are obstructive, restrictive and pulmonary vascular.
Obstructive, restrictive and vascular
Correct. As a diagnostic tool, pulmonary function tests help classify diffuse lung disease as obstructive, restrictive or pulmonary vascular (gas transfer impairment).
Mild, moderate and severe
Severity grades describe an obstruction once it is found; the three diagnostic categories are obstructive, restrictive and pulmonary vascular.
set2.cite: Pulmonary Function Testing - Prof. Fowler.pptx, Slides 6, 35 and 11

set2.io: Differentiate obstructive and restrictive pulmonary patterns.
set2.q: A 66-year-old nonsmoker has dyspnea on exertion, a dry cough, Velcro crackles and this chest film of small-volume lungs with reticular opacities. Which pulmonary function result would confirm the expected pattern?
opts: A low total lung capacity
Correct. Small-volume lungs with reticular opacities point to a restrictive (interstitial) process, a decrease in volume, and a low total lung capacity confirms restriction.
A high total lung capacity
Restriction is a decrease in volume, so its total lung capacity is low, not high.
A normal forced vital capacity
Restriction decreases the forced vital capacity; a normal one argues against it.
A slow rise with no plateau
A slow rise that never plateaus is the volume-time curve of severe obstruction; restriction has a normal-shaped curve with a lower plateau.
set2.cite: Pulmonary Function Testing - Prof. Fowler.pptx, Slides 3, 38, 41, 43 and 45

set2.io: Interpret basic pulmonary function study results.
set2.q: A 15-year-old boy with a spinal cord injury has had dyspnea for 2 months; his lungs are clear on auscultation. His pulmonary function report is shown, with reference values. Which reading of the report is correct?
opts: Restriction with a low diffusing capacity
The pattern is restriction, but his diffusing capacity is 97% of reference, above the normal floor of 60%, so gas transfer across the membrane is intact.
Obstruction with a normal diffusing capacity
Obstruction needs a ratio below 70%; his is 86%, equal to the reference, so getting air out is not the problem.
A mixed defect with a normal diffusing capacity
A mixed defect needs a low ratio as well as a low total lung capacity; his ratio of 86% is normal, so only restriction is present.
Restriction with a normal diffusing capacity

Correct. The FEV1/FVC (forced expiratory volume in one second over forced vital capacity) ratio is normal (86% against a reference of 86%) and the forced vital capacity (71%) and total lung capacity (67%) are low: restriction. The diffusing capacity, which measures the integrity of the alveolar-capillary membrane, is normal at 97%.

set2.alt: Pulmonary function report with spirometry, lung volumes, diffusing capacity and a small flow-volume loop

set2.io: Differentiate obstructive and restrictive pulmonary patterns.
set2.q: A 58-year-old man's forced breath out is traced as shown, with his FEV1/FVC (forced expiratory volume in one second over forced vital capacity) ratio printed on it (normal above 80%). Which pattern does it show?
opts: Gas transfer impairment
Gas transfer impairment keeps normal breathing mechanics and a normal ratio; a ratio of 47% is obstruction.
Normal lung mechanics
Normal mechanics puts more than 80% of the forced vital capacity out in the first second; here it is 47%.
Obstruction
Correct. A ratio of 47% is well below 70%, the marker of obstruction: too little of the forced vital capacity leaves in the first second.
Restriction
Restriction keeps the ratio normal or increased (70% or more); this ratio is 47%.

set2.alt: Tracing of lung volume against time during a forced breath out

set2.io: Differentiate obstructive and restrictive pulmonary patterns.
set2.q: A 61-year-old man's flow-volume loop is shown. Which pattern does it show?
opts: Normal
A normal loop is much wider along the volume axis; this one is narrow because the volume is reduced.
Severe obstruction
Severe obstruction has a low peak and a deeply scooped expiratory limb; this loop has a sharp, high point.
Obstructive
An obstructive loop has a scooped (coved) expiratory limb; this one is narrow with a straight, steep limb.
Restrictive
Correct. The loop is narrow and tall with a sharp point, like a witch's hat: everything is smaller because less volume moves, the restrictive pattern.
set2.cite: Pulmonary Function Testing - Prof. Fowler.pptx, Slide 44

set2.io: Describe pulmonary function testing parameters.
set2.q: A 55-year-old has this tracing of quiet breaths, one deepest breath in and one fullest breath out. Which volume does the shaded band represent?
opts: Tidal volume
Tidal volume is the small rise and fall of each quiet breath, near the middle of the tracing.
Residual volume
Correct. Below the lowest point of the fullest breath out lies the residual volume, the air still in the lung after maximal expiration; the tracing never enters it.
Functional residual capacity
Functional residual capacity is the residual volume plus the expiratory reserve volume above it, a taller band than this.
Expiratory reserve volume
The expiratory reserve volume is the band the fullest breath out does reach, just above the shaded one.
set2.cite: Pulmonary Function Testing - Prof. Fowler.pptx, Slides 20, 21 and 23
set2.alt: Spirometry tracing of lung volume against time with one band shaded yellow

set2.io: Describe pulmonary function testing parameters.
set2.q: A 61-year-old man with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis has worsening dyspnea. Which specialized test assesses his diaphragmatic strength?
opts: Peak expiratory flow measurement
Peak flow measures the maximum expiratory airflow in a single breath, as in asthma, not diaphragmatic strength.
Diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide
The diffusing capacity tests gas transfer across the alveolar-capillary membrane, not the strength of the diaphragm.
Whole-body plethysmography
Plethysmography measures lung volumes and airway resistance; muscle strength is tested by the maximal pressures.
Maximal inspiratory and expiratory pressures
Correct. Maximal inspiratory and expiratory pressures measure diaphragmatic strength and the neurologic side of breathing.
set2.cite: Pulmonary Function Testing - Prof. Fowler.pptx, Slides 19 and 13

set2.io: Describe pulmonary function testing parameters.
set2.q: A 40-year-old woman's spirometry gives values that do not fit her clinical picture. Besides correct patient technique and clean components, what does accurate testing depend on?
opts: Recording the lowest of the efforts
Of the three efforts the highest volumes and flows are recorded; accuracy rests on calibrated equipment, clean parts and technique.
Properly calibrated equipment
Correct. Accurate testing depends on properly calibrated equipment, clean components and correct patient technique; a calibration syringe is part of the equipment.
Testing only after a bronchodilator
Reports can show testing before and after a bronchodilator (albuterol), but neither replaces properly calibrated equipment.
A higher oxygen saturation first
Oxygen saturation is a separate measurement by pulse oximetry; accuracy of spirometry rests on calibration, clean parts and technique.
set2.cite: Pulmonary Function Testing - Prof. Fowler.pptx, Slides 12, 24 and 47

set2.io: Differentiate obstructive and restrictive pulmonary patterns.
set2.q: A 17-year-old boy with muscular dystrophy has a restrictive pattern on testing. What causes the restriction in his case?
opts: Increased airway resistance
Increased airway resistance is obstruction, not the restrictive pattern he has.
A damaged alveolar-capillary membrane
That is gas transfer impairment, which keeps normal breathing mechanics; his mechanics are what fail.
Weakness of the respiratory muscles
Correct. Neuromuscular diseases such as muscular dystrophy and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis impair lung function through weakness of the respiratory muscles rather than poor compliance.
Stiff lungs with poor compliance
Poor compliance is the route in interstitial lung disease; in neuromuscular disease the restriction comes from muscle weakness rather than poor compliance.
set2.cite: Pulmonary Function Testing - Prof. Fowler.pptx, Slide 8

set2.io: Explain the role of pulmonary function testing in diagnosis and monitoring of pulmonary disease.
set2.q: A 63-year-old man's spirometry suggests restriction. Which standard test is responsible for diagnosing restrictive lung disease?
opts: Repeat spirometry
Spirometry (with its flow-volume loop) is responsible for diagnosing obstructive disease; restriction is confirmed by lung volumes.
Lung volume measurement
Correct. Lung volumes are the standard test responsible for diagnosing restrictive lung disease; spirometry diagnoses obstruction and the diffusing capacity pulmonary vascular disease.
Diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide
The diffusing capacity tests the alveolar-capillary membrane and diagnoses pulmonary vascular disease, not restriction.
Peak flow monitoring
Peak flow is a bedside measure of maximum expiratory flow, used in asthma; it gives no lung volumes.
set2.cite: Pulmonary Function Testing - Prof. Fowler.pptx, Slides 18 and 43

set2.io: Discuss pulse oximetry and oxygenation assessment.
set2.q: A 65-year-old man with dyspnea has standard pulmonary function tests ordered, and a specialized test of oxygenation is added. Which of these is the specialized test?
opts: Diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide
The diffusing capacity is a standard test, responsible for diagnosing pulmonary vascular disease.
Spirometry with a flow-volume loop
Spirometry, with its flow-volume loop, is a standard test, responsible for diagnosing obstruction.
Lung volume measurement
Lung volumes are a standard test, responsible for diagnosing restriction.
An arterial blood gas
Correct. The arterial blood gas is listed among the specialized pulmonary function tests, with exercise oximetry, the six-minute walk, peak flow and the maximal pressures.
set2.cite: Pulmonary Function Testing - Prof. Fowler.pptx, Slides 19 and 18

set2.io: Differentiate obstructive and restrictive pulmonary patterns.
set2.q: A 66-year-old man's flow-volume loop is shown. Which pattern does it show?
opts: Gas transfer impairment
Gas transfer impairment keeps normal breathing mechanics and a normal-looking loop.
Normal
A normal expiratory limb runs in a straight line from the peak; this one bows inward.
Restrictive
A restrictive loop is narrow and pointed with a straight expiratory limb; this limb is scooped.
Obstructive
Correct. The expiratory limb is concave, scooped inward after the peak: the obstructive loop.
set2.cite: Pulmonary Function Testing - Prof. Fowler.pptx, Slides 36, 44 and 9

set2.io: Differentiate obstructive and restrictive pulmonary patterns.
set2.q: A 46-year-old woman has bronchiectasis with recurrent chest infections. Which pulmonary function pattern does her disease produce?
opts: Gas transfer impairment
Gas transfer impairment keeps normal breathing mechanics with a problem at the alveolar-capillary membrane; bronchiectasis raises airway resistance.
Restrictive
Restrictive physiology is poor compliance or neuromuscular impairment; bronchiectasis raises airway resistance instead.
Obstructive
Correct. Bronchiectasis is permanent airway dilation that results in chronic inflammation, recurrent infections and increased airway resistance: obstructive physiology.
Normal lung mechanics
Permanent airway dilation with increased airway resistance is not normal mechanics; it is obstruction.
set2.cite: Pulmonary Function Testing - Prof. Fowler.pptx, Slides 7 and 9

set2.io: Describe pulmonary function testing parameters.
set2.q: A 36-year-old man takes the deepest breath he can and then breathes out as fully as possible. Which capacity is the volume of that whole breath?
opts: Vital capacity
Correct. Vital capacity is the tidal volume plus the inspiratory and expiratory reserve volumes: every volume except the residual volume.
Total lung capacity
Total lung capacity also includes the residual volume, which stays in the lungs after the fullest breath out.
Inspiratory capacity
Inspiratory capacity is the breath in from the end of a quiet breath out; it leaves out the expiratory reserve volume.
Functional residual capacity
Functional residual capacity is the air left at the end of a quiet breath out, not the volume of a full breath.
